How much does a private trip cost?

It depends on the days, the number of travellers and where you stay. As a guide, for two travellers sharing: about €90–140 per person per day as a Wanderer, €220–270 as an Explorer and €490–580 in the Golden Fleece style. You get one final price in writing before you pay anything.
Will you help me prepare before I fly?
Yes. Once the plan is agreed, we send practical tips: entry rules, money and cards, a local SIM, and what to pack for the season and the places you’ll visit.
Is sending the form a booking?
No. It’s a request. We write back with ideas and questions, plan the route with you and only then confirm dates and price.
How and when do I pay?
A deposit confirms your trip once you accept the written quote; the balance is due by the date in your quote, usually a few weeks before you arrive. Nothing is paid online through this site.
What if I need to change or cancel?

Tell us as early as possible. Changes are usually easy; cancellation charges depend on how close to the trip you cancel and are set out in your quote and our booking terms. Plans change, and we’d rather adjust the trip than lose you.

Meet us at the airport. An evening walk through the old town's carved balconies and sulphur-bath domes ends at a welcome dinner — your first supra toast to the journey ahead.

Drive south to the basalt promontory where, in 1991, archaeologists found the first bones of the earliest humans known outside Africa. The ancient capital and a city of stone

Mtskheta, capital of the kingdom of Iberia and heart of Georgian Christianity: Jvari Monastery on its cliff and Svetitskhoveli Cathedral below. In the afternoon, Uplistsikhe — halls, a theatre and wine presses cut into the rock over many centuries.

Through the Mtkvari canyon past Khertvisi fortress to Vardzia: hundreds of rooms, chapels and wine cellars carved into the Erusheti mountainside in the 12th century. Inside the Church of the Dormition, a fresco of Queen Tamar painted in her lifetime still looks back at you.
Morning at Rabati Castle, where a church, a mosque and a synagogue share the same walls. Then cross into western Georgia — ancient Colchis, land of the Golden Fleece — arriving in Kutaisi for dinner.
Dinosaurs, a golden age, and a king's tomb

At Sataplia, walk above footprints left by dinosaurs in the Cretaceous mud. Then Gelati: founded in 1106 by King David the Builder as a monastery and academy, gleaming with medieval mosaics, and the place he chose to be buried — under the gate, so every visitor would step over him.
Drive back east across the country with a long lunch on the way. A farewell dinner — and if the timing works, polyphonic singing — in Tbilisi before your flight.

The history of Georgia: 1.8 million years in one scroll.

Few countries can tell the human story from its very first chapter. Georgia can: the first humans outside Africa, the first wine, one of the first Christian kingdoms, an alphabet all its own — and a hospitality that survived everything.
Start the storyExplore tours
Empires came from every direction — Persian, Roman, Arab, Byzantine, Mongol, Ottoman, Russian. Georgians kept their language, their faith, their songs and their wine. Walk through it with us.

On a basalt promontory at Dmanisi, south of Tbilisi, archaeologists have found the remains of the earliest humans known outside Africa — five skulls and many more bones, dated to roughly 1.85–1.77 million years ago.

Skull 5, published in 2013, is the most complete early human skull of its age ever found. These people were small, tool-making early Homo — and they changed what scientists thought about when, and how, humans first left Africa.
Someone buries a jar of wine

At the Neolithic villages of Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveris Gora, about 50 km south of Tbilisi, pottery jars still carry the chemical signature of grape wine. Published in 2017, they are the earliest known evidence of grape winemaking anywhere on Earth.
The method Georgians still use — fermenting and ageing wine in egg-shaped clay qvevri buried in the ground — was inscribed by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2013.

Western Georgia was Colchis, a land so rich in gold that the Greeks set one of their greatest myths there: Jason and the Argonauts sailing east to steal the Golden Fleece from King Aeëtes, helped by his daughter Medea.
The gold was real. Excavations at Vani have uncovered extraordinary Colchian jewellery, and the ancient geographer Strabo described mountain people catching gold dust from rivers in fleeces.

In the east rose the kingdom the Greeks and Romans called Iberia — Kartli to Georgians — with its capital at Mtskheta, where two rivers meet. Medieval chronicles credit its first king, Pharnavaz, with uniting the land.
For centuries Iberia balanced between Rome and Persia, trading along routes that would later be called the Silk Road.

According to tradition, a young woman named Nino came from Cappadocia carrying a cross made of grapevine branches, bound with her own hair. She converted Queen Nana and King Mirian III, and in the early 4th century Kartli became one of the first kingdoms in the world to adopt Christianity as its state religion.
The vine cross of St Nino is still the symbol of the Georgian Church. Her resting place is at Bodbe, above the vineyards of Kakheti.

Georgian has an alphabet entirely its own — rounded, curling letters you will see nowhere else on Earth. The oldest securely dated inscriptions are from the 5th century — including those at Bolnisi Sioni, dated 493–494.
A playful approximation — Georgian has sounds English doesn’t, and vice versa. (მოგზაური means “traveller”.)
Three scripts grew from it: Asomtavruli, Nuskhuri and today’s flowing Mkhedruli. In 2016 UNESCO inscribed the living culture of all three writing systems as Intangible Cultural Heritage.
Legend says King Vakhtang Gorgasali was hunting when a pheasant his falcon had caught fell into a hot spring. He ordered a city built on the spot and named it Tbilisi — from tbili, warm.
The sulphur springs still flow beneath the brick domes of the Abanotubani bath quarter.

King David IV inherited a weak, half-occupied kingdom and rebuilt it. On 12 August 1121, at Didgori, his army defeated a much larger Seljuk coalition; the next year he took back Tbilisi and made it his capital.
He founded Gelati Monastery and its academy in 1106 — and asked to be buried beneath its gate, so that everyone who entered would walk over him.
The golden age of King Tamar

His great-granddaughter Tamar ruled as mepe — king, not queen — over Georgia’s golden age, when its influence stretched across the Caucasus. The cliff city of Vardzia flourished under her, and her portrait is still on its church wall.
Shota Rustaveli dedicated his epic, The Knight in the Panther’s Skin, to her. Georgians still quote it, and many brides were once given a copy as part of their dowry.
Invasions, and a culture that endured

Mongol armies arrived in the 1220s; Timur invaded repeatedly between 1386 and 1403. The united kingdom eventually broke into smaller kingdoms and principalities, contested by Persian and Ottoman empires.

In the high valleys of Svaneti, families built stone defensive towers — most between the 9th and 12th centuries — and kept icons, manuscripts and treasures safe through it all. Upper Svaneti is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

In 1783 King Erekle II of Kartli-Kakheti signed the Treaty of Georgievsk, placing his kingdom under Russian protection. In 1801 the Russian Empire annexed it, and in the decades after, the rest of Georgia.

The 19th century brought a cultural revival: writers like Ilia Chavchavadze — now remembered as the father of the modern nation — and, at Tsinandali, Alexander Chavchavadze’s estate, where European-style wine met Georgian tradition.
A republic, and a long Soviet century
On 26 May 1918 Georgia declared independence as the Democratic Republic of Georgia. In 1921 the Red Army invaded, and Georgia spent the next seventy years inside the Soviet Union.
In 1977 a Georgian folk song, Chakrulo, was chosen for the Golden Record carried into deep space by the Voyager probes — Georgian polyphony is now travelling beyond the solar system.
On 9 April 1991 Georgia restored its independence. Today it welcomes travellers from all over the world — citizens of around 95 countries can visit without a visa, many for up to a year.
And it still keeps the old rule: a guest is a gift from God. The million-and-first step through this land could be yours.
Jason and the Argonauts sailed to Colchis — western Georgia — for a ram’s fleece of gold. One theory traces the myth to Svan villagers who laid sheepskins in mountain streams to catch gold dust.

Greek myth chained Prometheus to a peak in the Caucasus for giving fire to humans; Georgian tradition places him on Kazbek. Georgians have their own fire-thief hero, Amirani, chained in a mountain cave.
When God divided the earth, the Georgians arrived late — they had been feasting and toasting Him. Charmed, God gave them the land He had been keeping for Himself.
St Nino walked into Georgia carrying a cross of grapevines tied with her own hair. Wine and faith have been bound together here ever since.
Heritage the whole world signed up for.
Three writing systems of the Georgian alphabet2016

This history was written for Million First Steps from established sources — UNESCO, the Georgian National Museum, and peer-reviewed research on Dmanisi and early winemaking. Dates for the deep past are approximate, and scholars still debate some of them; that is part of the fun.

Georgia in ten points: what surprises first-time visitors · Million First Steps
1. A guest is a gift from God. Georgians say it and mean it. Expect to be fed, toasted and sent home with a bottle of somebody's grandfather's wine.
2. The alphabet is unique. Thirty-three rounded letters you will see nowhere else on Earth. Gamarjoba means hello, madloba means thank you.
3. Wine is 8,000 years old here. The oldest known traces of grape wine come from villages near Tbilisi, and families still make it in clay qvevri buried in the ground.
4. Cards work in cities, cash in villages. The currency is the lari (GEL). Carry some cash for markets, guesthouses and the mountains.
5. A local SIM costs little. Buy one at the airport with your passport, or use an eSIM. Coverage is good almost everywhere.
6. Khachapuri and khinkali come first. Cheese bread with an egg on top, and soup dumplings you eat with your hands. Georgian cooking is also full of vegetarian dishes.
7. The supra has rules. A feast is led by a tamada, the toastmaster. Wait for the toast before you drink your wine.
8. Churches have a dress code. Cover shoulders and knees; women usually cover their hair. Scarves are often available at the door.
9. Distances are short, roads are slow. Georgia is about the size of Ireland, but mountain roads wind. Plan two or three regions for a week, not six.
10. It feels safe and warm. Georgia is widely regarded as a safe country for travellers. Many older people speak Russian, and more and more young people speak English.

Do I need a visa for Georgia? · Million First Steps

Citizens of around 95 countries — including the EU, the UK, the USA, Canada and Australia — can visit Georgia without a visa, most of them for up to a year. Your passport should be valid for the whole of your stay.
Visitors from other countries can usually apply online through Georgia's official e-visa portal. Allow a few weeks before you travel, and keep a copy of the visa with your passport.

Entry rules change from time to time. Always check the list on the website of Georgia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, or ask the Georgian embassy in your country. If anything is unclear, tell us your nationality and we'll help you find the current rule.

Tbilisi, Kutaisi or Batumi: which airport? · Million First Steps

The main gateway, about 20 minutes from the city centre. Most full-service airlines fly here, with connections through Istanbul, Dubai, Doha, Warsaw, Munich and other hubs. The best choice if your trip starts in Tbilisi, Kakheti or Kazbegi.

In western Georgia, served mainly by low-cost airlines with direct flights from many European cities. Kutaisi is a good start for Imereti, Svaneti and the canyons; the drive to Tbilisi takes about three and a half hours.
On the Black Sea coast, with more flights in summer. Convenient for a trip that begins or ends at the sea.
Flying in to one, out of another
Open-jaw tickets often save a day of driving — for example, arriving in Kutaisi and leaving from Tbilisi. Whichever airport you choose, we meet you at arrivals and see you off when you fly home.
When to go: seasons and weather · Million First Steps
Green valleys, blossom and comfortable temperatures — lovely for Tbilisi, Kakheti, the cave towns and the canyons. The high mountains still have snow.

The season for the high Caucasus: Kazbegi, Svaneti and Tusheti, whose only road opens roughly from mid-June to early October. Tbilisi can be hot in July and August, and the Black Sea is warm enough for swimming from June to September.
Many people's favourite: golden light, mild days and the grape harvest, rtveli, in Kakheti. The mountains are still open until early October.
Skiing in Gudauri and Svaneti, quiet snowy monasteries and cosy wine cellars. The road to Kazbegi can close for a few hours in storms, and Tusheti is cut off until spring.
Getting around: drivers, trains and marshrutkas · Million First Steps

The easiest way to see the country, and how all our journeys work: a driver who knows the roads, stops where you want and waits while you explore. Mountain roads are narrow and winding, and local driving can be lively, so we don't recommend renting a car for a first visit.
Comfortable modern trains link Tbilisi with Batumi in about five hours, with slower services to Kutaisi and a scenic narrow-gauge line from Borjomi. Tickets sell out in summer, so book ahead.
Minibuses that connect almost every town and village. They are cheap and frequent but crowded, with no fixed timetable on many routes — an adventure rather than a plan.
Taxis booked through ride-hailing apps are inexpensive in Tbilisi and Batumi, and Tbilisi has a metro. The old town is best explored on foot.
Money, cards and tipping · Million First Steps
Georgia's currency is the lari (GEL, ₾). Exchange offices in cities offer fair rates, and ATMs are easy to find in every town.
Cards and contactless payments work almost everywhere in cities, hotels and restaurants. Carry some cash for village guesthouses, markets, small shops and the mountains.

Many restaurants add a 10% service charge to the bill, so check before you tip. Otherwise, rounding up is appreciated but never expected. For guides and drivers, a tip at the end of the trip is a kind gesture, not an obligation.
SIM cards and internet · Million First Steps
The main mobile networks have desks at Tbilisi airport and shops in every town. Bring your passport; a SIM with plenty of data costs little and works in minutes.
If your phone supports eSIM, you can buy a Georgian or regional data plan online before you fly and be connected the moment you land.
Mobile internet is fast in towns and along the main roads. In remote mountain valleys like Tusheti, coverage is patchy — part of the charm. Most hotels, cafés and guesthouses have Wi-Fi.
Staying safe and emergency numbers · Million First Steps

Georgia is widely regarded as a safe destination, and violent crime against visitors is rare. Use the same common sense as anywhere: keep an eye on your belongings in crowded places and use registered taxis at night.
Dial 112 for police, ambulance or fire. On our journeys, our team is reachable 24/7, and your guide is with you on the road.
Mountain weather changes fast and roads wind — which is why we drive. Bring warm layers even in summer, and follow your guide's advice on trails and river crossings.

Check your own government's travel advice before you travel. Two regions, Abkhazia and Samachablo (South Ossetia), are not under the control of the Georgian government and can't be visited from Georgia.
Supra etiquette: toasts and the tamada · Million First Steps

Every supra — a Georgian feast — is led by a tamada, the toastmaster. He or she proposes toasts in a traditional order: to peace, to the ancestors, to friendship, to the guests and much more. A supra can last all night. Pace yourself.

Wait for the tamada's toast before you drink your wine, then raise your glass: gaumarjos, cheers! Never toast with beer — that is traditionally reserved for enemies. If you'd rather not drink, a sip, or water, is perfectly fine; a polite no is always respected.

Dishes keep arriving and plates are stacked on top of each other — it's a sign of generosity, not a mistake. Eat khinkali with your hands: hold the knot, bite, sip the broth, then eat the rest, and leave the knot on your plate.
What to pack (and what to wear in churches) · Million First Steps

Bring layers: days can be warm and nights cool, especially in the mountains, where you'll want a fleece and a light rain jacket even in summer. Comfortable walking shoes are essential for old towns and trails.
Cover shoulders and knees. Women usually cover their hair, so a light scarf is handy; scarves and wraps are often available at the door. Men take off their hats.
Sun protection, a refillable water bottle and a power adapter for European two-pin plugs (types C and F, 220 V). Medicines you need, with a copy of the prescription.

Million First Steps is a small, family-run Georgian travel company. We plan every journey ourselves, and we treat every traveller as a guest at our own table.

One of us has spent a lifetime on Georgia's roads and knows which village bakery is still warm at dawn. The other grew up being dragged along — and now can't stop showing the country off to anyone who will listen.
“We think your steps should be the next ones. The million-and-first.”

About 1.8 million years ago, early humans walked out of Africa and into the hills of what is now Georgia. Their bones, found at Dmanisi, are the oldest human fossils ever discovered outside Africa. Since then, Georgia has been crossed by traders on the Silk Road, Greek sailors chasing a golden fleece, saints, poets and armies — a million footsteps, give or take.

How Million First Steps handles your personal data. No cookies, no tracking.
Short version: this website doesn’t track you. We only receive the details you choose to send us, and we use them only to plan your trip.
Million First Steps, Tbilisi, Georgia — “we”, “us”. Contact: hello@millionfirststeps.ge.
No cookies for visitors and no advertising trackers. We don’t use Google Analytics, Facebook pixels or similar tools.

Anonymous visit counts. Our own server counts page views — which page, the website you came from, your language and the kind of device — without cookies and without storing your IP address. If your browser sends a “Do Not Track” or “Global Privacy Control” signal, you aren’t counted.

Fonts and scripts are hosted on this website. Your browser does not contact Google Fonts, map services or any other third party when you visit. The “Open in Google Maps” link only takes you to Google if you click it.

Your preferences stay on your device. Your language, your travel style and whether you closed a notice are remembered in your browser’s local storage. They never leave your device and you can clear them at any time.
Our web host keeps standard server logs (such as IP address and pages requested) for security and to keep the site running.
When you send us a request

If you use one of our forms or write to us, we receive what you give us: typically your name, email address, phone number, travel dates, party size, the places you’d like to see and any notes (such as dietary or mobility needs). Forms are sent to our inbox by our website host’s mail server; if that isn’t available, the form opens your own email program instead.
Each request is emailed to us and kept in our booking system on our web host’s servers, which only our team can sign in to.

We use these details only to reply to you, to plan and operate your journey, and — once you book — to meet our legal and accounting obligations. To run your trip we share only what’s needed with the hotels, drivers and guides who host you. We never sell your data or use it for advertising.
Requests that don’t lead to a booking are deleted within 24 months. Booking records are kept for as long as tax and accounting law requires.

You can ask to see, correct or delete your data, or object to how we use it, by emailing us. If you are in Georgia, the Law of Georgia on Personal Data Protection applies; if you are in the EU/EEA or UK, you also have rights under the GDPR, including the right to complain to your local data protection authority.
Booking terms for Million First Steps journeys.
The small print, in plain words

These terms are being finalised before we accept our first bookings. Until then, the written quote we send you sets out the conditions for your trip — nothing is binding until you have read it and confirmed.

Prices on this website are “from” prices per person, based on two travellers sharing, and are for guidance. Your exact price depends on dates, party size and availability, and is confirmed in writing in your personal quote.
Your journey is confirmed when you accept your quote and we receive the deposit stated in it. The balance is due by the date in your quote, usually a few weeks before arrival.

Want to change something? Tell us as early as possible and we'll do our best — some changes may affect the price. If you need to cancel, the charges depend on how close to departure you cancel and on what we have already paid to hotels and partners; the exact scale is set out in your quote.
If we ever have to change a significant part of your trip, we'll offer an equivalent alternative or a refund for the affected part.
Comprehensive travel insurance, including medical cover and cancellation, is required for every traveller.

Some journeys include mountain roads and hikes at altitude. Please tell us about any health or mobility needs so we can plan safely. Your guide may adapt a route for weather or safety — their decision is final.
If something isn't right during your trip, tell your guide or call us straight away so we can fix it while you're here. After your trip, write to us at hello@millionfirststeps.ge.
These terms are governed by the laws of Georgia. This does not remove any rights you may have under the consumer laws of your own country.

This website doesn’t use cookies for visitors.
We don’t set cookies for visitors and we don’t load anyone else’s analytics, advertising or social media trackers — which is also why you didn’t see a cookie banner.
The only cookies on this site are a few for our own team on the staff area (to sign in and remember their language); visitors never get them.
